cards: Finnish and Estonian are cousins from the same small family. Many basic words match, but a lot of everyday ones don't.
Beware the false friends: in Finnish, 'hallitus' means government. In Estonian, it means mould.
Indonesian is a standardised form of Malay, so the basics are identical. The modern words drifted apart.
Careful with 'percuma': in Malaysia it means free of charge. In Indonesia it means useless.
Serbs and Croats understand each other completely. Most linguists call it one language with two standards, politics call it two.
The big difference is on paper: Serbian can be written in Cyrillic or Latin letters, Croatian only in Latin.
Turks and Azerbaijanis can chat without a translator. Azerbaijani was simply called Turkish until the Soviets renamed it in the 1930s.
The slogan says it all: one nation, two states.
Lao people understand Thai easily, they grow up watching Thai TV. Thais understand Lao a bit less.
About 20 million people in north-east Thailand speak Isan, which is basically Lao. So Lao has more speakers in Thailand than in Laos.
On paper they share about 89% of their vocabulary. In real life, Portuguese speakers understand Spanish much better than the other way round.
Why? Portuguese has more vowel sounds and swallows syllables, so Spanish ears get lost.
Bulgaria officially considers Macedonian a dialect of Bulgarian. North Macedonia strongly disagrees.
Both dropped the noun cases that every other Slavic language still has, and both put 'the' at the end of the word.
Czechoslovakia split in 1993, but TV shows are still broadcast in both languages without subtitles.
Older people understand each other perfectly. Young Czechs, who grew up without Slovak TV, are starting to struggle.
Norway was ruled by Denmark for 400 years, so written Norwegian is almost Danish. The sound is another story.
Danes swallow their consonants, so Norwegians read Danish easily but struggle to hear it. The joke: Norwegian is Danish spoken in Swedish.
Afrikaans grew out of the Dutch spoken at the Cape in the 1600s. Dutch speakers can read it almost without trying.
It threw away most of the grammar: no genders, no verb endings. Dutch 'ik ben, jij bent, hij is' becomes 'ek is, jy is, hy is'.
Spoken on the street, Hindi and Urdu are the same language: Bollywood films are understood in Pakistan word for word.
The split is in writing and in formal words: Hindi uses the Devanagari script and Sanskrit words, Urdu uses the Arabic script and Persian words.
